# Khadiraṅgārajātaka (Ja 40)

**ID:** Ja 40
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Khadiraṅgārajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Pit of Acacia Charcoal
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja40
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Khadiraṅgārajātaka* (Ja 40) is a story found in the first division of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral; Berkwitz 2006]. Set at Jetavana, the introductory narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*) concerns the great patron Anāthapiṇḍika, who had given so lavishly to the Buddha and the Saṅgha that he was reduced to poverty (*daliddiyappatta*) [SuttaCentral; Fenn 1994; Mus 1935]. A spirit (*devatā*) dwelling in his doorway tries to deter him from further charity, but Anāthapiṇḍika rejects her counsel and evicts the spirit, who must appeal to higher authorities such as the Four Great Kings (*Cātummahārājāno*) to regain her abode [Fenn 1994; Clark 1994; Mus 1935]. This introductory account of Anāthapiṇḍika was later incorporated into the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Burlingame 1921a].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Buddha recounts a previous life as a wealthy merchant whose determination to offer alms to a Paccekabuddha was tested by Māra [Burlingame 1921b; Francis 2002; Clark 1994]. Māra manifested a fiery pit of glowing acacia charcoal to prevent the almsgiving, yet the Bodhisatta fearlessly stepped forth, proclaiming that he would rather plunge headlong into hell than abandon an honorable act of giving alms [SuttaCentral; Burlingame 1921b; Clark 1994]. The Sinhala *Thūpavaṃsa* cites this narrative to exemplify the Bodhisatta’s perfection of giving (*dāna*) [Berkwitz 2006].

DharmaNexus identifies no significant Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels with score ≥10, and SuttaCentral records no direct parallels in other languages [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Beyond its textual transmission, the scene of Māra obstructing the feeding of the Paccekabuddha appears in the artistic relief program at Amarāvatī [Francis 2002], and details from the story have been cited by modern historians regarding the ancient Indian practice of stamping clay seals over pots of valuables [Olivelle 2006].
